title: Graphs, Tables & Data
coreInsight: Graphs and tables encode relationships; scale, position, shape, and change all carry mathematical meaning.
targetLearnerRealization: A graph tells a story about variables: slope, flatness, intersections, and scale must be interpreted in context rather than as a literal picture.
learningObjectives: Interpret graph segments as changes in related variables rather than pictures of physical paths.
Read axis labels and scales before comparing values.
Distinguish current height from rate of change.
Translate between tables, graphs, and contextual trends.

continuity.openingCallback: Replace a compressed numerical summary with a display that preserves when and how the values change.
closingSeeds: A constant rate appears as a straight line with constant steepness.
Coordinates and equations can describe every point on a line.

misconceptionTargets.misconception: A graph is a picture of a real scene rather than a representation of variables.
A taller point or bar always means a faster rate of change.
Reading one value is the same as understanding the trend.

beats.purpose: Translate one story event into variable behavior before showing the full authentic graph choices.
beats.expectedRealization: If time advances while distance stays fixed, a distance-time graph is horizontal.
beats.transitionIn: A single mean hid when values changed. A graph can keep time visible—but only if we read what each direction measures.
beats.prompt: A runner stops for a rest. Time continues, but distance from the start does not change. What should a distance-versus-time graph do during the rest?

options.text: Rise, because time is passing.
Stay horizontal, because distance is unchanged.
Fall, because the runner is tired.
Disappear, because the runner stopped.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Moving right records passing time; unchanged height records unchanged distance.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Track each variable separately: time changes, distance does not.

steps.body: Horizontal motion on the page does not mean the runner moves horizontally. It means the horizontal-axis variable changes while the vertical-axis variable stays constant.

resolution.takeaway: Read a graph as two variables changing together, not as a picture of the path.

beats.purpose: Build graph features from a motion story and eliminate choices one requirement at a time.
beats.expectedRealization: Steady motion, rest, direction, and finish order each impose a distinct graph condition.
beats.transitionIn: Keep the flat-rest rule. Now combine it with steady motion and a finish order in a complete race story.
beats.whyNow: The authentic tortoise-and-hare problem makes the core representational misconceptions visible in one coherent distance-time story.
beats.entryBridge: Translate each sentence into a requirement before judging any whole graph.
beats.exitBridge: One graph survives because every segment and endpoint matches a variable behavior in the story.
beats.reusedRepresentation: A distance-time display built event by event.
learnerPrompts: At the race step, watch which animal moves steadily and where the hare's distance freezes.
At the first elimination step, reject any tortoise line whose steepness changes.
At the second elimination step, require a flat hare segment and reject a downward segment as moving backward.
At the final comparison, identify which animal reaches the finish distance at the earlier time.
beats.correctFeedback: Yes. Graph B alone shows a steady tortoise, a hare who rests without moving backward, and the tortoise finishing first.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Test the choices in pieces: steady tortoise, flat hare nap, no backward motion, then finish order.

steps.title: Steady tortoise
steps.body: A constant slow pace requires one straight rising line, eliminating D.

steps.title: Hare's nap
steps.body: A stop requires a horizontal segment. E never stops, while C moves downward and therefore back toward the start.

steps.title: Finish order
steps.body: A and B have suitable shapes, but only B has the tortoise reach the finish distance first. The answer is B.

resolution.takeaway: Translate story clauses into graph properties, then test every property.

beats.purpose: Separate a graph's geometric appearance from the physical scene it represents.
beats.expectedRealization: A downward distance-time segment means distance decreases, not merely slowing or traveling downhill.
beats.transitionIn: One race choice sloped downward. Name what that geometry says about the variables.
beats.prompt: On a graph of distance from home versus time, what does a downward segment mean?

options.text: The traveler is moving downhill.
The traveler is slowing down but still moving away.
The distance from home is decreasing as time passes.
Time is moving backward.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The vertical variable decreases, so the traveler is getting closer to home.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Read the axis variables rather than imagining the drawn line as terrain.

steps.body: As the graph moves right, time increases. If it moves downward, the vertical quantity—distance from home—decreases. The physical road could be flat, uphill, or downhill; the graph does not show terrain.

resolution.takeaway: Graph direction describes variable change, not the shape of the real path.

beats.purpose: Make axis scale essential to reading a plotted value.
beats.expectedRealization: Tick spacing has numerical meaning and cannot be treated as one unit automatically.
beats.transitionIn: Graph direction tells how a variable changes. Tick labels tell how much it changes.
beats.prompt: The plotted point is at time 3 and height 60. What value does it show?

visual.ariaLabel: A graph with minutes from zero to four and liters from zero to one hundred in steps of twenty, with a point at three minutes and sixty liters

options.text: 3 liters
6 liters
20 liters
60 liters

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. The vertical ticks count by 20, placing the point at 60 liters.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Read the vertical tick labels and their step size before reading the point's height.

steps.body: The vertical labels are 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100. At time 3, the point aligns with 60 liters.

resolution.takeaway: Read labels, units, and tick steps before interpreting position.

beats.purpose: Distinguish a current amount from its rate of change.
beats.expectedRealization: A lower line can be changing faster than a higher line.
beats.transitionIn: Height answers “how much now.” Steepness answers “how fast is it changing.”
beats.prompt: At noon, Tank A contains 80 liters and is gaining 4 liters per minute. Tank B contains 60 liters and is gaining 7 liters per minute. Which statement is true?

options.text: Tank A's graph is higher, but Tank B's graph is steeper.
Tank A's graph is both higher and steeper.
Tank B's graph is higher because 7 > 4.
The two graphs must have equal steepness.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Eighty exceeds sixty, but seven liters per minute exceeds four liters per minute.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Separate the current liters from the liters added per minute.

steps.title: Compare height
steps.body: At noon, Tank A has the greater amount: 80 liters versus 60.

steps.title: Compare rate
steps.body: Tank B changes faster: 7 liters per minute versus 4, so its line is steeper.

resolution.takeaway: Height represents amount; steepness represents rate of change.

beats.purpose: Translate a table's repeated change into a graph description.
beats.expectedRealization: Equal input steps with equal output changes produce a steady straight trend.
beats.transitionIn: A table can expose exact values; compare successive rows to predict the graph's shape.
beats.prompt: A table lists time 0, 2, 4, 6 minutes and distance 0, 3, 6, 9 meters. Which graph description matches?

options.text: A straight rising line through the four points.
A horizontal line because the time steps are equal.
A falling line because 2 is less than 3.
Four unrelated points with no trend.

beats.correctFeedback: Right. Every 2-minute increase adds 3 meters, so the rate and steepness stay constant.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Compare each row with the next: the same time increase produces the same distance increase.

visual.ariaLabel: Four table points aligned on a straight rising distance-time graph

steps.body: The points (0,0), (2,3), (4,6), and (6,9) align because each equal run of 2 minutes has the same rise of 3 meters.

resolution.takeaway: Repeated change in a table becomes constant steepness on a graph.

beats.purpose: Name the representational features after learners have used them.
beats.expectedRealization: Axes, scale, points, segments, and trends each encode distinct information.
beats.transitionIn: The race, tank, and table displays all used the same visual grammar.
beats.name: Variables, axes, scale, and trend
beats.conciseDefinition: Axes name the related variables and units; scale assigns values to positions; points record paired values; segments and overall shape show how the relationship changes.
beats.formalization: horizontal change = input change; vertical change = output change; steepness compares the two changes

beats.purpose: Require interpretation of a multi-point display beyond reading one value.
beats.expectedRealization: A trend statement must account for the sequence of values, including reversals or flat portions.
beats.transitionIn: Use the visual grammar on data that rises and then falls rather than moving at one steady rate.
beats.prompt: Which statement best describes the full temperature pattern?

visual.ariaLabel: Temperature points rising from eighteen to twenty-seven degrees and then falling to twenty degrees

options.text: Temperature rises throughout all four hours.
Temperature falls throughout all four hours.
Temperature rises to a peak after 2 hours, then falls.
Temperature never changes because all points share one graph.

beats.correctFeedback: Correct. The full sequence rises to 27°C and then reverses downward.
beats.incorrectFeedback: Read the points from left to right and note where the direction changes.

steps.title: Read the rise
steps.body: The values move from 18 to 23 to 27°C during the first two hours.

steps.title: Read the reversal
steps.body: They then fall to 25 and 20°C. One value alone would miss the peak and change in direction.

resolution.takeaway: A trend describes the relationship across values, not just one point.

beats.purpose: Consolidate variable, scale, height, rate, and trend interpretation.
beats.expectedRealization: Reliable graph reading is a sequence of contextual checks.
beats.transitionIn: Every display became trustworthy only after several questions were answered in order.

options.text: Name both axis variables and units.
Read tick values before comparing heights.
Separate current amount from rate of change.
Treat the line as a literal picture of the physical path.
Use one point to describe every trend.

response.feedback: Keep the checks that connect visual features to named variables and discard picture-reading shortcuts.

beats.correctFeedback: Exactly. Context, scale, and change turn marks on a page into mathematical meaning.
beats.incorrectFeedback: A graph encodes variables; it is not scenery, and one point cannot reveal a whole trend.

steps.title: Orient
steps.body: Read variable names, units, and scales.

steps.title: Decode
steps.body: Interpret point height as amount and segment steepness as rate of change.

steps.title: Synthesize
steps.body: Follow the full display to describe flat portions, reversals, intersections, and trends.

beats.purpose: Create the successor need to connect a constant-rate line with coordinates and an equation.
beats.expectedRealization: A line's repeated rise and run can be encoded as a numerical rule.
beats.transitionIn: The table's straight line rose 3 meters whenever time ran 2 minutes. That repeated move can become a rule.
beats.prompt: What should a rule for that distance-time line preserve?

options.text: Every coordinate pair and the constant rise of 3 for each run of 2.
Only the final point, while ignoring all earlier points.
The visual color but none of the values.
A different rate between every pair of points.

beats.correctFeedback: Yes. One equation should generate every point while preserving the line's constant rate.
beats.incorrectFeedback: The rule must describe the entire straight relationship, not one isolated feature.

steps.body: Coordinates name each plotted pair, and the constant rise/run gives the line's slope. Connecting those pieces to an equation will let one symbolic rule describe the entire graph.

resolution.takeaway: A constant-rate graph invites a coordinate rule for the whole line.

notes: The approved tortoise-and-hare problem is the discovery anchor; later checks vary scale, variables, and representations.
The lesson remains draft pending human pedagogical review.
